tool.name: ExtractAspectValuesToPoints

summary.para:
View online help files: https://www.jennessent.com/topographic-analysis/extract-aspect-values-to-points.html
Adds a field holding the aspect value at each point, extracted from an aspect raster, to a copy of the input point features or to the input feature class itself -- like Esri's Extract Values to Points, but built for aspect: the optional interpolation is a bilinear weighted mean direction (a circular interpolation, never a linear average), flat cells (-1) are handled correctly, D-infinity flow-direction rasters are supported, and no Spatial Analyst is required. The raster can also be a DEM: the aspect is then computed at each point by Horn's 3 x 3 method (the method of Esri's Aspect tool) or a least-squares quadratic over a chosen window, over true ground distances in any coordinate system.

tool.usage:
Why a special tool for aspect. Aspect is a circular variable: 0 and 360 degrees are the same direction, and 359 and 1 are two degrees apart. An ordinary interpolated extraction (such as Esri's Extract Values to Points with interpolation on) averages the neighboring cell values linearly, so a point between a 359-degree cell and a 1-degree cell would get roughly 180 -- due south, the exact opposite of the correct roughly-north answer. This tool instead treats each neighboring cell as a unit vector and computes a bilinear weighted mean direction: the sines and cosines of the four surrounding cell centers are weighted by the standard bilinear weights, summed, and converted back to a direction. The result is always a true direction in compass degrees. (See the tool help for the Aspect Focal Statistics tool, and Jenness, J. 2012. Issues with directional data. Remotely Wild, newsletter of the Spatial Ecology and Telemetry Working Group of The Wildlife Society, for why aspect matters ecologically and why circular methods are required.)
Extraction options. With interpolation off (the default, matching Esri's default) each point receives the value of the raster cell it falls in, exactly as stored -- including -1 for a flat cell. With interpolation on, each point receives the weighted mean direction of the four surrounding cell centers as described above. Flat cells (aspect -1) carry no direction, so they are excluded from the interpolation and the weights are renormalized over the remaining directional neighbors; if every contributing neighbor is flat the point receives -1; NoData neighbors are likewise excluded. Points on NoData or outside the raster receive NULL in a geodatabase output, or -9999 in a shapefile (which cannot store null). The tool warns if the raster's values fall outside the aspect range (-1 to 360 degrees), which usually means the input is not an aspect raster.
Where the values go. A new point feature class: a copy of the input points (an active selection and definition query are honored) carrying all the input attributes plus one new DOUBLE field holding the extracted value in compass degrees. A new field in the input feature class: the field is added to the input itself and no copy is made; the points the layer shows (its selection and definition query) receive values and any other rows of the feature class are left NULL, and the run report says how many. A layer with a join cannot take a new field. In either case the field is named "Aspect" unless you choose another name; a name that is not valid for the workspace, or is already taken, is adjusted (Aspect_2, Aspect_3, ...) and the run messages report the name actually used. Esri's option to append all the raster's attributes is deliberately not offered. The field's metadata records the units, the -1 and NULL/-9999 conventions, the extraction method, and the source raster.
Coordinate systems. The points are read in the raster's coordinate system (the raster is never projected -- projecting a raster damages it; reprojecting point coordinates is exact), and the raster is read only over the points' extent, so large regional rasters are handled efficiently. Projected and geographic rasters both work.
D-infinity flow direction. A D-infinity (DINF) flow-direction raster is essentially an aspect raster -- the direction of steepest descent -- but in the mathematical convention (0 = east, increasing counter-clockwise) rather than compass, which most users do not realize. Set "Input aspect convention" to Mathematical for such a raster and the extracted values are converted to compass degrees. The tool suggests this setting automatically when it detects a DINF raster from the geoprocessing history. (A standard D8 flow-direction raster stores flow codes 1-128, not degrees, and is not valid input.)
Computing from a DEM. Set What the raster holds to Elevation (DEM) and the tool derives the aspect itself, at exactly the cells the sampling step needs, so the numbers are the same as making an aspect raster first and extracting from it. The default Horn (3 x 3) method is the third-order finite difference used by Esri's Aspect tool (planar method), down to its NoData rule and its -1 for flat cells; on a projection that is true to scale, such as UTM or State Plane, the values are identical to extracting from an Esri planar aspect raster. The distances between cells are measured on the spheroid whatever the coordinate system, so a Web Mercator or a lat/long DEM works too (see the help site's page on projection distortion). The Quadratic least squares method fits the Evans-Young quadratic surface to a window of 3 to 15 cells and takes the aspect from its first derivatives at the center; a wider window smooths and generalizes. Like Esri's Aspect tool, the directions are measured from the grid's north: on a projected DEM that differs from true north by the grid convergence, under a degree for UTM but several degrees for a continental conic projection. Elevation units default from the DEM's vertical coordinate system when it has one; the Input aspect convention does not apply to a DEM (values are compass degrees). To extract values computed exactly as Esri's Surface Parameters tool computes them, run Surface Parameters first and extract from its raster.
Values are always written in compass degrees (0 = north, clockwise); -1 = flat. This tool honors no geoprocessing environments. References: circular statistics follow Mardia and Jupp (2000), Fisher (1993), Batschelet (1981), and Zar (1999); see also Jenness (2012).

dialogReference.para: The point features to extract aspect values for. An active selection is honored. Must be a single-point feature class (multipoint is not supported).

param.name: in_raster
param.displayname: Input aspect raster or DEM (single band)

dialogReference.para: A single-band aspect raster in degrees, 0-360 measured clockwise from north (compass), with -1 for flat cells (a D-infinity flow-direction raster is also valid input: set the Input aspect convention to Mathematical for it; the tool warns if the values fall outside the -1 to 360 range) -- or a DEM, with What the raster holds set to Elevation (DEM), in which case the aspect is computed from the elevations at each point.

Aspect values (default): the raster already holds aspect. Elevation (DEM): the raster holds elevations and the tool computes the aspect itself with the method chosen below (see Computing from a DEM in the usage notes); the values are compass degrees with -1 for flat, as from Esri's Aspect tool.

A new point feature class (a copy of the input): the input points are copied to the output feature class and the field is added to the copy. A new field in the input feature class: the field is added to the input itself and no copy is made; the output feature class parameter is then disabled. Only the points the layer shows receive values; other rows stay NULL.

The new point feature class: a copy of the input points with all their attributes plus the new aspect field. A name is suggested from the input. Required when the values go to a new feature class; ignored when they go into the input.

param.name: interpolate
param.displayname: Interpolate values at the point locations (weighted mean direction)

dialogReference.para: Unchecked (default): each point gets the value of the cell it falls in, exactly as stored (including -1 for flat). Checked: each point gets a bilinear weighted mean direction interpolated from the four surrounding cell centers -- a circular interpolation in which each neighbor's direction is treated as a unit vector, so directions near north interpolate correctly (359 and 1 give roughly 0, never 180). Flat and NoData neighbors are excluded and the weights renormalized; all-flat neighbors give -1.

The name of the new DOUBLE field holding the extracted aspect (default "Aspect"). Adjusted automatically if the name is invalid for the workspace or already taken; the dialog warns when the input already has a field of that name.

The angular convention of the input raster. Choose Compass for an ordinary aspect raster (0 = north, increasing clockwise). Choose Mathematical for a D-infinity (DINF) flow-direction raster: DINF reports the direction of steepest descent -- essentially aspect -- but in the mathematical convention (0 = east, increasing counter-clockwise), which most users do not realize. With Mathematical selected the extracted values are converted to compass degrees. The tool suggests this setting automatically when it detects a DINF raster.

Only when the raster is a DEM. Horn (3 x 3) (default): the third-order finite difference of Esri's Slope and Aspect tools, over true ground distances; on a true-to-scale projection it gives exactly the numbers Esri's planar tool gives. Quadratic least squares: the Evans-Young quadratic surface fitted to a window of cells (choose the size below), the aspect taken from its first derivatives at the center; a wider window smooths noisy, fine-resolution DEMs.

The square window the quadratic surface is fitted to, 3 to 15 cells on a side (odd numbers). Only used with the quadratic method; Horn's method is always 3 x 3. Larger windows average over more terrain, as Esri's Surface Parameters neighborhood distance does.

The DEM's elevation unit, Meters or Feet. Set automatically, and locked, when the DEM has a vertical coordinate system that says; choose it yourself otherwise. A wrong unit scales every aspect value, so check it when the DEM's metadata is silent.
For ModelBuilder: the input point features with their new field, filled in when the values are written into the input feature class (empty when a new feature class is made).

scriptExample.title: Extract Aspect Values to Points example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Extract the containing-cell aspect into a copy of the points, then a circular-interpolated aspect into a new field of the input itself. interpolate: True or False. write_to: "A new point feature class (a copy of the input)" or "A new field in the input feature class". input_convention: "Compass (0 = north, clockwise)", "Mathematical (0 = east, counter-clockwise; e.g. D-infinity)". The new field is DOUBLE, compass degrees; -1 = flat; NULL (geodatabase) or -9999 (shapefile) = NoData or outside the raster.
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
# Value of the cell each point falls in (no interpolation), written to a copy of the points arcpy.jenness.ExtractAspectValuesToPoints( in_points=r"C:\Project\Wildlife.gdb\telemetry_points", in_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\aspect", surface_type="Aspect values", write_to="A new point feature class (a copy of the input)", out_points=r"C:\Project\Wildlife.gdb\telemetry_points_Aspect", interpolate=False, field_name="Aspect", input_convention="Compass (0 = north, clockwise)")
# Circular (weighted mean direction) interpolation, written into the input feature class arcpy.jenness.ExtractAspectValuesToPoints( in_points=r"C:\Project\Wildlife.gdb\telemetry_points", in_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\aspect", surface_type="Aspect values", write_to="A new field in the input feature class", interpolate=True, field_name="Aspect")
# Aspect straight from a DEM: Horn's 3 x 3 method, the numbers Esri's Aspect tool gives arcpy.jenness.ExtractAspectValuesToPoints( in_points=r"C:\Project\Wildlife.gdb\telemetry_points", in_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\dem", surface_type="Elevation (DEM)", write_to="A new field in the input feature class", interpolate=False, field_name="Aspect", slope_method="Horn (3 x 3; the method of Esri's Slope and Aspect tools)", elev_units="Meters")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Adds a field with the aspect at each point from an aspect raster, to a copy of the points or to the input feature class itself -- containing-cell value or bilinear weighted-mean-direction (circular) interpolation; flat (-1) handled correctly; D-infinity supported; no Spatial Analyst.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: The circular analog of Esri's Extract Values to Points. Aspect is a circular variable, so an ordinary interpolated extraction averages neighboring values linearly and puts ~180 between 359 and 1; this tool instead computes a bilinear weighted mean direction (unit vectors of the four surrounding cell centers, bilinearly weighted, resultant converted back to a direction). Flat cells (aspect -1) are excluded from interpolation with weights renormalized; all-flat neighbors give -1; NoData or outside-the-raster points get NULL (geodatabase) or -9999 (shapefile). Points are read in the raster's coordinate system (the raster is never projected) and the raster is read only over the points' extent. D-infinity flow-direction rasters -- essentially aspect in the mathematical convention -- are supported via a convention toggle that converts values to compass. The field goes to a copy of the input points, with all their attributes, or into the input feature class itself, under a name you choose; one new DOUBLE field is added with full field-level metadata. Circular statistics follow Mardia and Jupp (2000), Fisher (1993), Batschelet (1981), and Zar (1999); see Jenness (2012).
dataIdInfo.idCredit: Tool by Jeff Jenness, Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com). Methods: Mardia, K. V., and P. E. Jupp. 2000. Directional Statistics (Wiley); Fisher, N. I. 1993. Statistical Analysis of Circular Data (Cambridge Univ. Press); Batschelet, E. 1981. Circular Statistics in Biology (Academic Press); Zar, J. H. 1999. Biostatistical Analysis, 4th ed. (Prentice Hall). See also Jenness, J. 2012. Issues with directional data. Remotely Wild, newsletter of the Spatial Ecology and Telemetry Working Group of The Wildlife Society. Suggested citation: Jenness, J. (2026). Extract Aspect Values to Points. Jenness Enterprises Wildlife and Forestry Tools for ArcGIS Pro. Available at: http://www.jennessent.com.
